doc.title: Derek Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 5, 2021

title: First heroes Kenny G and Dave Koz, playing along in the garage
summary: His first saxophone CDs were Kenny G and Dave Koz; he played along with transcription books in the cold garage.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Was there a first saxophone player that you heard and you wondered, all right, who is that, and then you started looking for that name?
Yup, all right, so here is where some people are going to judge me, but whatever, I’m going to let it all out.
Now you’re going to say Boots Randolph, right?

Nope. I’m going to go even further. Because yeah I actually wasn’t introduced to Boots until much later. But I’m actually going to go all the way smooth jazz and I’ll say, like I said I was born in ’83, I listened to lot of pop music growing up, so the big name if you want to guess. Kenny G.

Him and then even more I think my first two saxophone CDs I was given was Kenny G and Dave Koz, so another smooth jazz guy. And I remember, and like I said, I grew up with pop. This was basically pop so this made sense to me, but it was done by a saxophone. It was done by the instrument that I’m playing. And it sounded really good to me. And I’m really grateful for those first two CDs because it was that music that got me to kind of, I think, break outside of the box in the way of like kind of taking it as my own instead of being given music in assignments from my private lesson teacher, which is great, you’ve got to start somewhere, or my band teacher. I’m just doing what they asked me to do. Here I was given a CD and wasn’t asked to do anything with it and yet I

wanted to like, hey are there transcription books with this? I want to play along with this. And then I remember taking the CD and this little boom box that I had and I would go out to the garage, and this was in Michigan and in the winter it would get really cold in the garage, but it didn’t matter, I would go in that garage because it had the best acoustics in the house, you know this nice reverb. And I would put on that Dave Koz and I had my little transcription book and I would just close my eyes and play. And it got me also to kind of play out, like I don’t listen so much to smooth jazz these days, but a lot of the tone of these musicians is really nice. And I think a lot of people could learn from the tone of smooth jazz players. Just kind of like really putting air through the horn and making a beautiful sound. And listening to those albums, I would close my eyes and play along and I’d kind of like have the dream of like man I could do this on a stage one day, you know, this is great. And it was, once again, it wasn’t an assignment, it was me doing something for the first time on my own with music. It seems small but I think it was a big step.
